items.title: Greeting with an f-string
items.prompt: Write `greet(name, n)` that returns `'Hi Ada, you have 3 new messages'`.
hints: Python's template strings start with f before the quote.
Inside an f-string, put expressions in {curly braces}.
return f"Hi {name}, you have ... new messages"
items.solution:
def greet(name, n):
    return f"Hi {name}, you have {n} new messages"
items.lesson: f-strings are Python's template literals: f"{expr}". Format specs go after a colon: f"{price:.2f}".

items.title: Money with a format spec
items.prompt: Write `money(x)` that returns e.g. `'$1,234.50'` for `1234.5` (thousands separator, 2 decimals).
hints: The format spec goes after a colon inside the braces: {x:SPEC}.
'.2f' means two decimals; a comma before it adds thousands separators.
return f"${x:,.2f}"
items.solution:
def money(x):
    return f"${x:,.2f}"
items.lesson: Format specs live after the colon: `:,.2f` (thousands + 2 decimals), `:>8` (right-align), `:02d` (zero-pad), `:.1%` (percent).

items.title: Slugify a title
items.prompt:
Write `slugify(title)`: trim surrounding whitespace, lowercase, and replace spaces with `-`.

`'  Hello World '` → `'hello-world'`
hints: Strings have methods for each step; they return new strings (strings are immutable).
The methods are .strip(), .lower() and .replace(old, new). Chain them.
return title.strip().lower().replace(" ", "-")
items.solution:
def slugify(title):
    return title.strip().lower().replace(" ", "-")
items.lesson: `strip` = JS `trim`, `lower` = `toLowerCase`, `replace` replaces ALL occurrences by default (unlike JS `replace` with a string).

items.title: Reverse the words
items.prompt: Write `reverse_words(s)`: `'the quick  fox'` → `'fox quick the'` (collapse extra spaces).
hints: split() with no argument splits on any run of whitespace and drops empties.
Reverse the list with a slice, then glue it back with a string's join method.
return " ".join(s.split()[::-1])
items.solution:
def reverse_words(s):
    return " ".join(s.split()[::-1])
items.lesson: In Python `join` is a method on the separator: `" ".join(parts)`. `s.split()` (no arg) handles any whitespace run.

items.title: Palindrome check
items.prompt:
Write `is_palindrome(s)` that ignores case and anything that is not a letter or digit.

`'A man, a plan, a canal: Panama'` → `True`
hints: First build a cleaned, lowercased string; then compare it with its reverse.
c.isalnum() tests a character; "".join(... for c in s) builds the cleaned string; s[::-1] reverses.
t = "".join(c.lower() for c in s if c.isalnum()); return t == t[::-1]
items.lesson: `s[::-1]` reverses any sequence. A generator inside `"".join(...)` is the idiomatic way to filter characters.

items.title: Squares of the evens
items.prompt: Write `even_squares(nums)` returning the squares of the even numbers, in order, in ONE expression.
hints: A list comprehension is [expression for item in iterable if condition].
Even means n % 2 == 0; square is n * n or n ** 2.
return [n * n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0]
items.solution:
def even_squares(nums):
    return [n * n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0]
items.lesson: `[expr for x in xs if cond]` replaces `.filter().map()`. Read it left to right: what you produce, then where it comes from, then the filter.

items.title: Flatten a grid
items.prompt: Write `flatten(grid)`: `[[1, 2], [3], []]` → `[1, 2, 3]`, using a single comprehension.
hints: Two `for` clauses can live in one comprehension.
The for clauses go in the same order as nested loops: outer first.
return [x for row in grid for x in row]
items.solution:
def flatten(grid):
    return [x for row in grid for x in row]
items.lesson: Nested comprehensions read like nested loops written on one line: `[x for row in grid for x in row]` — outer loop first.

items.title: Count words with dict.get
items.prompt: Write `count_words(words)` returning a dict word → count, using a plain dict (no imports).
hints: Loop over words and bump a counter for each one.
d.get(key, default) returns the default instead of raising KeyError.
counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1
items.lesson: `d[k]` raises KeyError for a missing key; `d.get(k, 0)` doesn't. (Week 2: `collections.Counter` does this for you.)

items.title: Invert a dict
items.prompt: Write `invert(d)` that swaps keys and values: `{'a': 1, 'b': 2}` → `{1: 'a', 2: 'b'}`.
hints: A dict comprehension uses braces and key: value.
d.items() yields (key, value) pairs you can unpack in the for clause.
return {v: k for k, v in d.items()}
items.solution:
def invert(d):
    return {v: k for k, v in d.items()}
items.lesson: `{k: v for ...}` builds a dict; iterate `d.items()` to get key and value together (plain `for k in d` gives keys only).

items.title: Common elements
items.prompt: Write `common(a, b)` returning the values present in both lists, sorted ascending, without duplicates.
hints: Turn both lists into sets.
The & operator is set intersection; sorted() turns any iterable into a sorted list.
return sorted(set(a) & set(b))
items.solution:
def common(a, b):
    return sorted(set(a) & set(b))
items.lesson: Sets have operators: `&` intersection, `|` union, `-` difference, `^` symmetric difference. Membership is O(1) on average.
items.ts: [...new Set(a)].filter(x => new Set(b).has(x)).sort((x, y) => x - y)

items.title: Numbered list
items.prompt: Write `numbered(items)`: `['eggs', 'milk']` → `['1. eggs', '2. milk']`.
hints: Don't use range(len(items)): there's a builtin that yields (index, item).
enumerate(items, start=1) starts counting at 1.
return [f"{i}. {x}" for i, x in enumerate(items, start=1)]
items.solution:
def numbered(items):
    return [f"{i}. {x}" for i, x in enumerate(items, start=1)]
items.lesson: `enumerate(xs, start=1)` gives (index, value) pairs — Python's answer to `forEach((x, i) => ...)`.

items.title: Zip into a dict
items.prompt: Write `to_dict(keys, values)`: `(['a', 'b'], [1, 2])` → `{'a': 1, 'b': 2}`. One line.
hints: There's a builtin that walks two iterables in lockstep.
zip(keys, values) yields pairs; dict() accepts an iterable of pairs.
return dict(zip(keys, values))
items.solution:
def to_dict(keys, values):
    return dict(zip(keys, values))
items.lesson: `zip(a, b)` pairs items and stops at the shortest input (`zip(a, b, strict=True)` raises instead). `dict(pairs)` builds a dict.

items.title: FizzBuzz to 15 (print it)
items.prompt: At top level, PRINT the numbers 1..15, one per line, but `Fizz` for multiples of 3, `Buzz` for 5, `FizzBuzz` for both.
items.tests:
EXPECTED = ["1", "2", "Fizz", "4", "Buzz", "Fizz", "7", "8", "Fizz", "Buzz",
            "11", "Fizz", "13", "14", "FizzBuzz"]
def test_output():
    got = captured_output.split()
    assert got == EXPECTED, f"expected {EXPECTED}, printed {got}"
hints: range(1, 16) stops BEFORE 16. Use % to test divisibility.
Check the 'both' case first (i % 15 == 0), then 3, then 5, else the number.
if i % 15 == 0: print("FizzBuzz") / elif i % 3 == 0: ... / elif i % 5 == 0: ... / else: print(i)
items.lesson: `range(a, b)` is half-open [a, b). It's `elif`, not `else if`. `print` adds a newline itself.

items.title: Longest first, ties alphabetical
items.prompt: Write `longest_first(words)`: sort by length descending; equal lengths in alphabetical order.
items.tests:
def test_basic():
    got = longest_first(["bb", "a", "ccc", "aa"])
    assert got == ["ccc", "aa", "bb", "a"], f"got {got!r}"
def test_no_mutation():
    w = ["b", "aa"]
    longest_first(w)
    assert w == ["b", "aa"], "don't sort the caller's list in place"
hints: sorted() returns a new list and takes a key= function.
A key can return a tuple: it compares element by element. Negate the length to get descending.
return sorted(words, key=lambda w: (-len(w), w))
items.solution:
def longest_first(words):
    return sorted(words, key=lambda w: (-len(w), w))
items.lesson: Python sorts with `key=` (a one-arg function), not a comparator. Tuple keys give multi-level sorts; `-x` flips one level.

items.title: Oldest person
items.prompt: `people` is a list of dicts like `{'name': 'Ada', 'age': 36}`. Write `oldest(people)` returning the NAME of the oldest.
hints: max() takes the same key= argument as sorted().
The key gets one person dict and returns what to compare: p["age"].
return max(people, key=lambda p: p["age"])["name"]
items.solution:
def oldest(people):
    return max(people, key=lambda p: p["age"])["name"]
items.lesson: `max(xs, key=f)` / `min(xs, key=f)` return the ELEMENT with the biggest f(x) — no reduce needed. Add `default=` for empty inputs.

items.title: Defaults and keyword args
items.prompt: Write `make_url(path, host='localhost', port=8000)` returning `'http://HOST:PORT/PATH'`.
hints: Default values go in the signature: def f(a, b=1).
Callers can skip host and pass port=9000 by name; your signature needs both defaults.
def make_url(path, host="localhost", port=8000): return f"http://{host}:{port}/{path}"
items.solution:
def make_url(path, host="localhost", port=8000):
    return f"http://{host}:{port}/{path}"
items.lesson: Any parameter can be passed by name (`port=9000`), so Python rarely needs an options object. Defaults must come after non-defaults.

items.title: Sum any number of args
items.prompt: Write `total(...)` so that `total()` → 0, `total(1, 2, 3)` → 6.
hints: A starred parameter collects extra positional args into a tuple.
def total(*nums): ... and nums is a tuple; sum() adds an iterable.
def total(*nums): return sum(nums)
items.solution:
def total(*nums):
    return sum(nums)
items.lesson: `*args` collects positionals into a tuple (TS rest params). At the CALL site, `f(*xs)` spreads a list and `f(**d)` spreads a dict.
items.ts: function total(...nums: number[]) { return nums.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) }

items.title: HTML tag with **kwargs
items.prompt: Write `tag(name, **attrs)`: `tag('a', href='/', id='x')` → `'<a href="/" id="x">'`. Keep the order the attrs were passed.
hints: **attrs collects keyword args into a dict (insertion order is kept).
Build ' key="value"' for each item in attrs.items() and join them.
parts = "".join(f' {k}="{v}"' for k, v in attrs.items()); return f"<{name}{parts}>"
items.lesson: `**kwargs` collects named args into a dict. Dicts keep insertion order (guaranteed since 3.7).
items.ts: function tag(name: string, attrs: Record<string, string> = {})

items.title: Force a keyword argument
items.prompt: Write `connect(host, timeout=5)` returning `f'{host}:{timeout}'`, but make `timeout` keyword-only: `connect('db', 10)` must raise TypeError.
hints: A bare marker in the parameter list makes everything after it keyword-only.
The marker is a lone star: def f(a, *, b=1).
def connect(host, *, timeout=5): return f"{host}:{timeout}"
items.solution:
def connect(host, *, timeout=5):
    return f"{host}:{timeout}"
items.lesson: A bare `*` in the signature forces the following params to be named — great for booleans and timeouts (`sort(key=..., reverse=True)` works this way).
items.ts: function connect(host: string, { timeout = 5 }: { timeout?: number } = {})

items.title: The main guard
items.prompt: Define `main()` that prints `ready`, and call it ONLY when the file is run as a script (not when imported).
items.tests:
import io, contextlib
def test_main_prints():
    buf = io.StringIO()
    with contextlib.redirect_stdout(buf):
        main()
    assert buf.getvalue().strip() == "ready", f"main() printed {buf.getvalue()!r}"
def test_not_run_on_import():
    assert captured_output == "", "main() ran on import — wrap the call in the __name__ check"
hints: Python sets a module-level variable to "__main__" only for the file you run directly.
if __name__ == "__main__": goes at the bottom, unindented.
def main(): print("ready")  then  if __name__ == "__main__": main()
items.lesson: `if __name__ == "__main__":` runs code only when the file is executed directly, so the module stays importable (and testable) without side effects.

items.title: Parse an int safely
items.prompt: Write `parse_int(s, default=0)` returning `int(s)`, or `default` if `s` isn't a valid integer.
hints: int('4x') raises an exception; catch that specific one.
The exception is ValueError. Avoid a bare except: it hides real bugs.
try: return int(s) / except ValueError: return default
items.lesson: Catch the narrowest exception (`except ValueError:`), never a bare `except:`. Python favours EAFP: try it, handle the failure.
items.ts: const n = Number.parseInt(s, 10); return Number.isNaN(n) ? def : n

items.title: Raise on bad input
items.prompt: Write `withdraw(balance, amount)` returning the new balance, but raise `ValueError('insufficient funds')` if `amount > balance`.
hints: Python uses raise, not throw.
Create the exception by calling the class with a message: ValueError("...").
if amount > balance: raise ValueError("insufficient funds")
items.lesson: `raise ValueError("msg")` — pick a built-in that fits (ValueError for bad values, TypeError for wrong types, KeyError for missing keys).
items.ts: if (amount > balance) throw new Error('insufficient funds')

items.title: try / except / else / finally
items.prompt: Write `safe_div(a, b, log)`: return `a / b`, or `None` on division by zero. Append to `log`: `'div0'` on error, `'ok'` on success, and ALWAYS `'done'` last.
items.tests:
def test_ok():
    log = []
    assert safe_div(6, 3, log) == 2, "6 / 3 should be 2"
    assert log == ["ok", "done"], f"log was {log}"
def test_zero():
    log = []
    assert safe_div(1, 0, log) is None, "division by zero returns None"
    assert log == ["div0", "done"], f"log was {log}"
hints: `else:` runs only if the try block raised nothing; `finally:` runs no matter what — even after return.
Put the division in try, catch ZeroDivisionError, log 'ok' in else, 'done' in finally.
try: r = a / b / except ZeroDivisionError: log.append("div0"); return None / else: log.append("ok"); return r / finally: log.append("done")
items.lesson: `else` keeps the happy path out of the try (so you don't accidentally catch its errors); `finally` is for cleanup and runs even after `return`.
items.ts: try { ... } catch (e) { ... } finally { ... }  // TS has no else clause

items.title: Seconds to HH:MM:SS
hints: // is integer division and % is remainder; divmod(a, b) returns both at once.
h, rest = divmod(seconds, 3600); m, s = divmod(rest, 60). Zero-pad with the format spec :02.
items.solution:
def to_hms(seconds):
    h, rest = divmod(seconds, 3600)
    m, s = divmod(rest, 60)
    return f"{h:02}:{m:02}:{s:02}"
items.lesson: `/` always gives a float in Python 3; `//` floors. `divmod(a, b)` returns `(a // b, a % b)` — unpack it directly.

items.question: What does this print?
items.explanation: s[::-1] reverses to 'nohtyp'; [:3] takes the first three characters.

items.question: What does this print?
items.explanation: Negative indexes count from the end. Slices are half-open: xs[1:-1] drops the first and last element.

items.question: What does this print?
items.explanation: Empty containers and zero are falsy. "0" is a non-empty string, so it's truthy. Same as JS except [] and {} — those are truthy in JS but falsy in Python.
items.ts: In JS, [] and {} are truthy; in Python they're falsy.

items.question: What does this print?
items.explanation: // floors toward negative infinity (so -7 // 2 is -4, not -3), and % takes the sign of the divisor (-7 % 3 is 2). / always returns a float.
items.ts: Math.trunc(-7 / 2) is -3 and -7 % 3 is -1 in JS — Python differs on both.

items.question: What does this print?
items.explanation: b = a copies the reference, so appending via b changes a. a[:] (or list(a) / a.copy()) makes a shallow copy, so c is independent.
items.code:
a = [1, 2]
b = a
b.append(3)
c = a[:]
c.append(4)
print(a)
items.ts: Same as JS: const b = a shares; [...a] copies.

items.question: What does this print?
items.explanation: A starred target collects the remaining items into a LIST (not a tuple). Unpacking works on any iterable; `a, b = b, a` is the swap idiom.

items.question: What does this print?
items.explanation: Braces without a colon make a SET comprehension, so duplicate lengths collapse. sorted() returns a list.
items.code:
words = ["hi", "yo", "hey", "a"]
print(sorted({len(w) for w in words}))

items.question: What does this print?
items.explanation: == compares values (deep, for lists); `is` compares identity. Use `is` only for None/True/False singletons: `if x is None:`.
items.code:
a = [1, 2]
b = [1, 2]
print(a == b, a is b, None is None)
items.ts: Python == on lists is like a deep-equal; `is` is like JS ===  on objects.

items.question: What does this print?
items.explanation: Strings are immutable: methods return a NEW string. s.upper() result is thrown away, so s is still 'abc'.
items.code:
s = "abc"
s.upper()
t = s.replace("b", "B")
print(s, t)
items.ts: Same in JS: s.toUpperCase() doesn't change s.

items.question: Time complexity of `x in my_list` vs `x in my_set` (n elements)?
items.explanation: `in` on a list scans every element. Sets and dicts hash the value, so lookup is O(1) on average. Convert to a set when you test membership in a loop.
items.ts: array.includes(x) is O(n); set.has(x) is O(1).

items.question: utils.py contains `print('A')` and then `if __name__ == "__main__": print('B')`. Another file does `import utils`. What prints?
items.explanation: When imported, the module's __name__ is 'utils', not '__main__', so the guarded block is skipped. Top-level code still runs on import.

items.title: Most frequent word
items.prompt: Arrange the lines so `most_frequent(text)` returns the most common lowercase word.
items.lesson: `max(d, key=d.get)` returns the key with the largest value — iterating a dict yields its keys.

items.title: Keep only valid ints
items.prompt: Arrange the lines so `to_ints(strs)` converts each string to int and skips the invalid ones.
items.lesson: Keep the `try` body tiny (just the line that can fail) and catch the specific exception; `continue` skips to the next item.

items.title: The list that remembers
items.fixed:
def add_item(item, bucket=None):
    bucket = [] if bucket is None else bucket
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket
choices: Default `bucket=None` and create a new list inside when it's None
Move `bucket=[]` to the first line of the body and keep the default
items.explanation: Default values are evaluated ONCE, when `def` runs, so every call shares the same list. Use `None` as the default and build a new list inside.

items.title: Top three scores
choices: Use `sorted(scores, reverse=True)` — `list.sort()` sorts in place and returns None
items.explanation: `list.sort()` mutates and returns `None` (unlike JS `arr.sort()`, which returns the array). `sorted(xs)` returns a new list and leaves the input alone.
